query: For a high-entropy alloy initially designed as a single-phase solid solution, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why it loses toughness or undergoes brittle fracture under mechanical loading in demanding engineering service? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, identify the applicable service and loading boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloys, demanding service that provides sufficient time at temperatures enabling lattice diffusion drives short-range ordering and multicomponent grain-boundary segregation, causing complexion transitions to lower-cohesion boundary states and, in some compositions, boundary-localized nanoscale intermetallic precipitation. These structural changes reduce grain-boundary cohesive strength and dislocation absorption capacity, shifting fracture from ductile transgranular to brittle intergranular under mechanical loading and thereby reducing toughness. The severity scales with exposure temperature (relative to alloy melting temperature) and time.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiaxed, solutionized single-phase solid-solution HEA (e.g., FCC-type with moderate stacking-fault energy), grain size ~10–50 µm, minimal second phases, clean boundaries, tested in inert environment; baseline exhibits ductile transgranular fracture and high impact energy and fracture toughness.
generation.intervention: Thermal aging at service-relevant temperature to activate diffusion (e.g., 0.35–0.50 Tm) for controlled durations, with or without low-amplitude cyclic mechanical loading during exposure, followed by mechanical toughness testing in the same inert environment and geometry as the baseline.
generation.conditions: Example controlled exposure: 0.40 Tm (absolute temperature based on alloy composition) for 200–1000 hours in vacuum or inert gas; mechanical tests at room temperature and subzero temperatures at strain rates ~10^-3–10^-2 s^-1; exclude hydrogen or corrosive media to isolate thermally driven effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Multicomponent grain-boundary segregation leading to complexion transition (e.g., nanoscale chemically ordered boundary layers) combined with short-range ordering/clustering in the grain interior; possible boundary-localized nano-precipitates of brittle intermetallic phases if composition permits.
generation.mechanism: Boundary segregation and ordering lower grain-boundary cohesive energy and reduce the ability of boundaries to absorb/emit dislocations, promoting early crack initiation at boundaries and intergranular crack propagation; interior short-range order reduces dynamic recovery and strain hardening, accelerating localization and facilitating boundary-controlled fracture.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline, thermally aged specimens will show a directional decrease in impact energy (moderate-to-large, approximately 25–60% lower depending on temperature and time), a measurable reduction in J-integral/K_IC fracture toughness, an upward shift in ductile-to-brittle transition temperature, and a change in fracture surface from predominantly ductile transgranular dimples to increased intergranular facets or quasi-cleavage. Atom probe/TEM will reveal increased boundary segregation and/or complexion features and interior short-range order or clustering. If boundary-localized nano-precipitates form, they will be concentrated at boundaries, correlating with intergranular crack paths.
generation.baseline: As-solutionized single-phase alloy tested without prior thermal exposure exhibits high toughness (high impact energy, stable crack growth in J-R curves), pronounced work hardening, and ductile transgranular fracture surfaces with microvoid coalescence and limited boundary faceting.
generation.boundary: Applicable when service involves temperatures ≥0.35–0.40 Tm and durations sufficient for multicomponent diffusion (tens to hundreds of hours) in inert or mildly reactive environments. Effects diminish at cryogenic or low-temperature service where diffusion is negligible, in alloys/compositions with intrinsically segregation-resistant boundaries, or when boundary character is dominated by special CSL boundaries that resist embrittlement. Additional embrittlement mechanisms (e.g., hydrogen, irradiation) can superimpose but are excluded in this hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of toughness loss and whether nano-precipitates form depend strongly on specific alloy chemistry and grain-boundary character distribution; some FCC HEAs may exhibit primarily short-range order without precipitation. Without alloy-specific data, quantitative ranges are approximate.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two cohorts from the same heat: (A) baseline solutionized single-phase specimens; (B) identical specimens thermally aged at 0.40 Tm for 500 h in high-purity Ar (no hydrogen) and optionally a second sub-cohort aged under the same thermal conditions with low-amplitude cyclic loading. Perform identical mechanical toughness tests (Charpy V-notch, J_IC/K_IC, tensile with fractography) and microstructural characterization (APT for boundary segregation, TEM/STEM for complexions and precipitates, nanoindentation or microcantilever tests for boundary cohesive strength).
measurements: Charpy V-notch impact energy at multiple temperatures (including subzero) to determine DBTT shifts
J_IC or K_IC and J-R curves under monotonic loading
Fractography quantifying fraction of intergranular versus transgranular fracture
Atom probe tomography maps of grain-boundary segregation profiles and interior short-range order indicators
TEM/STEM imaging of boundary complexions and any nano-precipitates (size, density, location)
Microcantilever or micro-GB cleavage tests to estimate boundary cohesive strength before/after aging
Hardening rate versus strain from tensile tests to detect changes in strain hardening
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if aged specimens do not exhibit any statistically significant reduction in toughness metrics (impact energy and J_IC/K_IC remain within baseline scatter) and do not show increased intergranular fracture fraction, while microstructural analyses reveal no increase in grain-boundary segregation/complexion features or short-range order relative to baseline. Alternatively, if toughness decreases but there is no detectable change in boundary segregation/complexions and fracture remains transgranular, the proposed boundary-mediated mechanism is falsified.
